```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 110)
```

## Summary

India has put a phone in almost every household. The harder question is **who
actually gets online, who benefits, and whether rising incomes fix the gaps on
their own.** Using about one million adults from the Government of India's
2022-23 CAMS survey, we find that:

1. **Phones are near-universal; computers are not.** 92% of the poorest fifth
   of households have a mobile phone against 98% of the richest, but only 0.9%
   of the poorest own a computer against 29.4% of the richest.
2. **The gender gap in internet use narrows with income but never closes.** A
   woman in the richest fifth of households (73.8%) is only level with a man in
   the fourth fifth (74.1%).
3. **The gap is generational.** For 15-24 year-olds in the richest fifth it is
   1.7 percentage points; for 35-44 year-olds in the poorest fifth it is 27.5.
4. **Money buys women connectivity, not work.** As household spending rises,
   women's internet use climbs steeply while their economic participation
   drifts down slightly (35.5% to 32.1%).
5. **Regression confirms it.** After controlling for income, age, education
   and sector, women still have about 54% lower odds of using the internet
   (odds ratio 0.46), and digital skill is linked to work mainly in the
   richest households.

**How the report is organised.** Part 1 is descriptive and uses survey weights,
so its figures describe the Indian population. Part 2 tests whether those
patterns are too large to be chance and whether they survive when several
factors are considered together.

**Colour key.** Teal = men, amber = women, throughout. Charts on income use a
light-to-dark teal scale, and the gap heatmap runs from cream to burnt orange.
The two sex colours are distinguishable for colour-blind readers too.

## Data and Reproducibility

**Source.** Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI),
National Sample Survey Office, 79th Round, *Comprehensive Annual Modular
Survey* (2022-23), unit-level data. We use the household, member and course
files.

**What is in this repository.** The raw files are very large, so
`prepare_data.R` reduces them to two compact analysis files (`data/`) holding
only the variables used here, for adults aged 15+ recorded as male or female.
Every derived variable is built in that script, so the pipeline from raw survey
to chart can be audited end to end.

```{r load-libraries}
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling and ggplot2
library(here)        # file paths that work on any computer
library(survey)      # survey weights and design
library(srvyr)       # survey tools in tidyverse style
library(broom)       # tidy model output
library(car)         # vif() multicollinearity checks
```

```{r load-data}
households <- readRDS(here("data", "cams_households.rds"))
members    <- readRDS(here("data", "cams_members.rds"))

# One palette, defined once, used everywhere
sex_cols <- c(Male = "#1F7A8C", Female = "#E9A03B")   # deep teal / warm amber
q_labels <- levels(households$mpce_quintile)
q_cols   <- colorRampPalette(c("#CFE8E4", "#1F5F6B"))(5)   # light to deep teal
```

**Households:** `r format(nrow(households), big.mark = ",")` &nbsp;|&nbsp;
**Adults (15+):** `r format(nrow(members), big.mark = ",")`

### Variables we constructed

* **Survey weight** = `MULT / 100`, as stated in the survey's readme.
* **Economic status.** Usual monthly consumer expenditure divided by household
  size gives **monthly per capita expenditure (MPCE)**, the standard measure of
  living standards in Indian survey work. Households are sorted into five equal
  groups (**quintiles**) from poorest to richest using *weighted* cut-offs, so
  each quintile represents a fifth of the population, not a fifth of the sample.
* **Digital capability score (0-4)** = owns a smartphone + can use the internet
  + can send email + can do digital banking. Someone is "Low" at 0-1,
  "Medium" at 2-3 and "High" at 4.
* **Skip-pattern correction.** The email and banking questions are asked only of
  people who can already use the internet, which is asked only of phone
  owners. A blank therefore means "skipped because the answer upstream was no",
  not "missing". Coding blanks as `NA` would silently drop 37.6% of adults, and
  precisely the least digital ones, biasing every result upwards. We code them
  as 0.
* **Education** is a simple flag for whether a person appears in the survey's
  course file at all. It is *not* years of schooling.
* **Sex of household head.** Devices are recorded per household, so household
  charts compare male-headed with female-headed households, not individual men
  and women.

```{r capability}
members <- members |>
  mutate(
    age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(14, 24, 34, 44, 59, 200),
                    labels = c("15-24", "25-34", "35-44", "45-59", "60+")),
    capability_score = mobile_smartphone + can_use_internet +
      can_email + can_digital_bank,
    capability_tier = factor(
      case_when(capability_score <= 1 ~ "Low",
                capability_score <= 3 ~ "Medium",
                TRUE ~ "High"),
      levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(members$capability_score), !anyNA(members$mpce_quintile))

hh_design     <- as_survey_design(households, ids = FSU, strata = stratum_1, weights = weight)
member_design <- as_survey_design(members,    ids = FSU, strata = stratum_1, weights = weight)
```

```{r validate-weights, include=FALSE}
hh_internet <- weighted.mean(households$has_internet == "Yes", households$weight)
```

**Validation check.** Our weighted estimate of household internet access is
**`r round(100 * hh_internet, 1)`%** (computed live from the data). The official
CAMS 2022-23 report gives 76.3%, so the import, weights and derived variables
are behaving correctly.

---

# Part 1: Descriptive Evidence (survey-weighted)

## 1. Who can afford to get online?

### Household access by sex of household head

```{r chart-1-bar}
access_by_head_sex <- hh_design |>
  filter(head_sex %in% c("Male", "Female")) |>
  group_by(head_sex) |>
  summarize(
    Mobile   = survey_mean(has_mobile == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100,
    Computer = survey_mean(has_computer == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100,
    Internet = survey_mean(has_internet == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Mobile, Computer, Internet), names_to = "device", values_to = "pct")

ggplot(access_by_head_sex, aes(device, pct, fill = head_sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Household digital access, by sex of household head",
       subtitle = "Describes the household's head, not individual men and women",
       x = NULL, y = "Households with access (%)", fill = "Household head") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Female-headed households look less connected. But a female-headed household is,
on average, also a poorer household, so before reading this as a gender effect
we look at spending power.

### Household access by spending power (MPCE quintile)

```{r chart-1b-bar}
access_by_quintile <- hh_design |>
  filter(!is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(mpce_quintile) |>
  summarize(
    Mobile   = survey_mean(has_mobile == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100,
    Computer = survey_mean(has_computer == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100,
    Internet = survey_mean(has_internet == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Mobile, Computer, Internet), names_to = "device", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(device = factor(device, levels = c("Mobile", "Internet", "Computer")))

ggplot(access_by_quintile, aes(mpce_quintile, pct, fill = mpce_quintile)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct, 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ device) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = q_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 105)) +
  labs(title = "Household digital access rises steeply with spending power",
       subtitle = "Monthly per capita expenditure quintiles, weighted",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Households with access (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**What this shows.** The three devices behave very differently. A mobile phone
is close to universal and barely moves with income (92.0% in the poorest fifth
to 97.8% in the richest). Internet access moves moderately (62.9% to 88.5%). A
computer is almost purely a function of money: **0.9% of the poorest fifth own
one against 29.4% of the richest, a gap of more than thirty times.** India has
not one digital divide but at least two: a shallow one for phones and a deep one
for the devices used to do skilled work.

### Does the sex-of-head gap survive once income is held roughly equal?

```{r chart-1c-line}
access_q_sex <- hh_design |>
  filter(head_sex %in% c("Male", "Female"), !is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(mpce_quintile, head_sex) |>
  summarize(Internet = survey_mean(has_internet == "Yes", vartype = NULL) * 100)

ggplot(access_q_sex, aes(mpce_quintile, Internet, colour = head_sex, group = head_sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Household internet access, by spending power and sex of head",
       subtitle = "The sex-of-head gap is small once households of similar means are compared",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Households with internet access (%)",
       colour = "Household head") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** The two lines sit close together at every income level.
Most of the apparent "female-headed households have less access" story is an
income story. The more interesting gender question is not whether a device
enters the house but **who in the house gets to use it**.

## 2. Within a household, who actually uses it?

### Digital skills by sex

```{r chart-2-bar}
use_by_sex <- member_design |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarize(
    `Smartphone use`  = 100 * survey_mean(mobile_smartphone == 1, vartype = NULL),
    `Internet use`    = 100 * survey_mean(can_use_internet == 1, vartype = NULL),
    `Email use`       = 100 * survey_mean(can_email == 1, vartype = NULL),
    `Digital banking` = 100 * survey_mean(can_digital_bank == 1, vartype = NULL)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-sex, names_to = "indicator", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(indicator = factor(indicator, levels = c("Smartphone use", "Internet use",
                                                  "Email use", "Digital banking")))

ggplot(use_by_sex, aes(indicator, pct, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Digital skills, by sex (individuals aged 15+)",
       x = NULL, y = "Percent able to do the task", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1))
```

### Internet use by sex and spending power

```{r chart-2b-bar}
net_by_q_sex <- member_design |>
  filter(!is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(mpce_quintile, sex) |>
  summarize(pct_net = 100 * survey_mean(can_use_internet == 1, vartype = NULL))

ggplot(net_by_q_sex, aes(mpce_quintile, pct_net, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct_net)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Internet use rises with income for both sexes, but the ladders never meet",
       subtitle = "Age 15+, weighted. Women in the richest fifth only match men in the fourth.",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Can use the internet (%)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** Income matters more than gender in raw size: moving from
the poorest to the richest fifth adds about 36 percentage points for women
(37.7% to 73.8%), while the gender gap at any income level is 12 to 17 points.
But the bars never level up. **A woman in the richest fifth of households
(73.8%) is only just level with a man in the fourth fifth (74.1%).**

### The size of the gap itself

```{r chart-2c-dumbbell}
gap_data <- net_by_q_sex |>
  select(mpce_quintile, sex, pct_net) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = pct_net) |>
  mutate(gap = Male - Female)

ggplot(gap_data, aes(y = fct_rev(mpce_quintile))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = Female, xend = Male, yend = fct_rev(mpce_quintile)),
               colour = "grey70", linewidth = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Female, colour = "Female"), size = 5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = Male, colour = "Male"), size = 5) +
  geom_text(aes(x = (Female + Male) / 2, label = paste0(round(gap, 1), " pp")),
            vjust = -1.3, size = 3.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "The digital gender gap narrows as households get richer",
       subtitle = "Gap in internet use, men minus women, percentage points (age 15+)",
       x = "Can use the internet (%)", y = "MPCE quintile", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** The gap falls from 16.6 points in the poorest fifth to 11.6
in the richest. That is real progress but slow: a 36-point rise in household
living standards buys only a 5-point cut in the gender gap.

### Capability by education and sex

```{r chart-3-bar}
cap_by_edu <- member_design |>
  group_by(has_course, sex) |>
  summarize(mean_cap = survey_mean(capability_score, vartype = NULL))

ggplot(cap_by_edu, aes(has_course, mean_cap, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_cap, 2)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Digital capability, by education and sex",
       subtitle = "Mean score out of 4, weighted. Education = appears in the course file.",
       x = "Has a course record", y = "Mean capability score (0-4)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Capability by income, sex and sector

```{r chart-3b-line}
cap_by_q_sex_sector <- member_design |>
  filter(!is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(sector, mpce_quintile, sex) |>
  summarize(mean_cap = survey_mean(capability_score, vartype = NULL))

ggplot(cap_by_q_sex_sector, aes(mpce_quintile, mean_cap, colour = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ sector) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Mean digital capability, by spending power, sex and sector",
       subtitle = "Score of 0-4. Rural women start lowest and stay lowest at every income level.",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Mean capability score (0-4)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** All lines slope upwards, so money raises capability
everywhere. But rural and urban panels sit at different levels: a rural
household has to be considerably richer to match an urban household's
capability. Rural women are the lowest line at every point on the income scale.

## 3. Where has the gap already closed?

### Capability across age groups

```{r chart-4-line}
capability_by_age_sex <- member_design |>
  group_by(age_group, sex) |>
  summarize(mean_capability = survey_mean(capability_score, vartype = NULL))

ggplot(capability_by_age_sex, aes(age_group, mean_capability, colour = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Mean digital capability score across age groups, by sex",
       subtitle = "Does the gap between the sexes widen or narrow with age?",
       x = "Age group", y = "Mean capability score (0-4)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### The gap by age *and* income

Each tile is one age-and-income cell. The number is how many percentage points
more men use the internet than women in that cell.

```{r chart-4b-heatmap}
gap_heat <- member_design |>
  filter(!is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(age_group, mpce_quintile, sex) |>
  summarize(pct_net = 100 * survey_mean(can_use_internet == 1, vartype = NULL)) |>
  select(age_group, mpce_quintile, sex, pct_net) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = pct_net) |>
  mutate(gap = Male - Female)

ggplot(gap_heat, aes(mpce_quintile, fct_rev(age_group), fill = gap)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(gap, 1)), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#FBF1DF", high = "#B5541C") +
  labs(title = "The digital gender gap, by age and spending power",
       subtitle = "Men's internet use minus women's, percentage points. Darker = wider gap.",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Age group", fill = "Gap (pp)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

**What this shows.** The gap is a landscape, not one number.

* Among **15-24 year-olds in the richest fifth the gap is 1.7 points**:
  effectively closed.
* The **worst cell is 35-44 year-olds in the poorest fifth, at 27.5 points**:
  the cohort that reached adulthood before cheap smartphones and lacked the
  money to catch up.
* For the young, money closes the gap fast (13.5 points in Q1 to 1.7 in Q5). For
  45-59 year-olds it barely helps.
* Among the **60+ the gap widens with income** (4.8 to 19.5 points). This is
  not a reversal: almost nobody in the poorest elderly group is online, so
  there is no room for a gap. A near-zero gap can mean equality or *shared
  exclusion*, and a chart like this is how you tell them apart.

### Who is online, by age

```{r chart-5-age}
age_net <- member_design |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarize(pct = 100 * survey_mean(can_use_internet == 1, vartype = NULL))

ggplot(age_net, aes(age_group, pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1F7A8C") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Share able to use the internet, by age group",
       subtitle = "Adults 15+, weighted, men and women combined",
       x = "Age group", y = "Can use the internet (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4. Does being online translate into economic participation?

"Economically active" means working or seeking work in the last 7 days.

### By capability tier and sex

```{r chart-6-bar}
econ_by_tier_sex <- member_design |>
  group_by(capability_tier, sex) |>
  summarize(pct_active = 100 * survey_mean(economically_active == "Yes", vartype = NULL))

ggplot(econ_by_tier_sex, aes(capability_tier, pct_active, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Economic participation, by digital capability tier and sex",
       subtitle = "Association only, not a causal claim",
       x = "Digital capability tier", y = "Economically active, last 7 days (%)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Does money buy women jobs the way it buys them internet?

```{r chart-6b-line}
econ_by_q_sex <- member_design |>
  filter(!is.na(mpce_quintile)) |>
  group_by(mpce_quintile, sex) |>
  summarize(
    `Can use the internet` = 100 * survey_mean(can_use_internet == 1, vartype = NULL),
    `Economically active`  = 100 * survey_mean(economically_active == "Yes", vartype = NULL)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`Can use the internet`, `Economically active`),
               names_to = "outcome", values_to = "pct")

ggplot(econ_by_q_sex, aes(mpce_quintile, pct, colour = sex, group = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(title = "Money buys women connectivity, but not work",
       subtitle = "Same people, same income scale, two very different outcomes (age 15+)",
       x = "MPCE quintile", y = "Percent", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** Women's internet use climbs from 37.7% to 73.8% as
households get richer, while women's economic participation *falls* slightly
(35.5% to 32.1%) and men's stays flat at roughly 74-80%. The same rise in
prosperity that puts a smartphone in a woman's hand is associated with her being
*less* likely to be in the labour force. This echoes a pattern long documented
in India's female labour-force-participation literature: women often withdraw
from low-paid manual work as household income rises, without a matching supply
of acceptable alternatives.

It also explains why digital skill looks unrelated to work in the previous
chart: many economically active people, in agriculture, construction and
informal trade, do not need digital skills for their jobs.

### Where does digital skill pay off?

```{r chart-6c-bar}
dividend <- member_design |>
  filter(mpce_quintile %in% q_labels[c(1, 5)]) |>
  group_by(mpce_quintile, capability_tier, sex) |>
  summarize(pct_active = 100 * survey_mean(economically_active == "Yes", vartype = NULL)) |>
  mutate(mpce_quintile = droplevels(mpce_quintile))

ggplot(dividend, aes(capability_tier, pct_active, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct_active)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ mpce_quintile) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 95)) +
  labs(title = "Digital skill pays off for women only in the richest households",
       subtitle = "Association only, not a causal claim",
       x = "Digital capability tier", y = "Economically active (%)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**What this shows.** In the poorest fifth, moving a woman from Low to High
capability is associated with *lower* participation (37.6% to 31.6%): digital
skill there mostly marks someone who is studying or outside manual work. In the
richest fifth the pattern flips: High-capability women are at 43.0%, against
24.2% in the Medium tier and 31.5% in the Low tier. The "digital dividend" for
women is concentrated where white-collar jobs exist. That is a labour-market
question, not a training question.

### By education and sex

```{r chart-7-bar}
econ_by_edu_sex <- member_design |>
  group_by(has_course, sex) |>
  summarize(pct_active = 100 * survey_mean(economically_active == "Yes", vartype = NULL))

ggplot(econ_by_edu_sex, aes(has_course, pct_active, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sex_cols) +
  labs(title = "Economic participation, by education and sex",
       x = "Has a course record", y = "Economically active (%)", fill = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

---

# Part 2: Formal Statistical Analysis

Part 1 describes the population. Part 2 asks two further questions: are these
patterns too large to be sampling noise, and do they survive when several
explanatory variables are considered together?

**Note on method.** The tests below use the individual-level data **without
survey weights**, so they describe relationships in the analysed sample. The
weighted figures in Part 1 are the population-representative estimates. With
about one million observations, almost any difference is statistically
significant, so we focus on the *size* of effects (odds ratios, differences in
means) rather than p-values alone.

## Research questions

**Research Question 1 (primary).** Does the gender gap in internet use persist once we control
for household spending power, age, education and sector, or is it explained
away? We test it with a sex-by-income interaction.

**Research Question 2 (secondary).** Is digital capability associated with economic
participation, and does that association depend on household income?

```{r reg-data}
reg_data <- members
nrow(reg_data)
```

## Do men and women differ in mean capability?

```{r ttest}
t.test(capability_score ~ sex, data = reg_data)
```

## Spending power and digital capability

```{r cor}
cor.test(reg_data$mpce, reg_data$capability_score)
```

## Two-way ANOVA: capability by income quintile and sex

```{r anova}
summary(aov(capability_score ~ mpce_quintile * sex, data = reg_data))
```

**What these three tests show.** Men's mean capability score is 2.05 against
1.44 for women, a gap of about 0.61 points on the 0-4 scale (p < 2.2e-16). The
correlation between MPCE and capability is 0.272: positive and significant, but
modest, so spending power alone is far from the whole story. The ANOVA shows
significant effects of income quintile, sex and their interaction, meaning the
size of the gender gap itself varies across income groups. ANOVA does not say
*which* quintiles differ; the regression below does.

## Regression 1: who can use the internet? (logistic)

`can_use_internet` is 0/1, so we use logistic regression. We build up in four
steps to see what each group of variables adds.

```{r logit-models}
models_internet <- list(
  model_1_sex_only      = can_use_internet ~ sex,
  model_2_add_income    = can_use_internet ~ sex + mpce_quintile,
  model_3_full_controls = can_use_internet ~ sex + mpce_quintile + age_group +
                            has_course + sector,
  model_4_sex_x_income  = can_use_internet ~ sex * mpce_quintile + age_group +
                            has_course + sector
) |>
  map(glm, data = reg_data, family = binomial)
```

```{r odds-ratios}
model_4 <- models_internet$model_4_sex_x_income

odds_ratios <- tidy(model_4, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  mutate(conf.low  = exp(log(estimate) - 1.96 * std.error),
         conf.high = exp(log(estimate) + 1.96 * std.error),
         term = str_replace_all(term, "\n", " ")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))

knitr::kable(odds_ratios,
             caption = "Model 4: odds ratios for being able to use the internet")
```

**Reading Model 4.** Reference groups: men, Q1 (poorest), age 15-24, no course
record, rural.

* **Sex.** The female odds ratio is 0.461 (p < 0.001): in the poorest quintile,
  women have about **54% lower odds** of using the internet than otherwise
  similar men.
* **Income.** Odds ratios rise from 1.461 (Q2) to 6.371 (Q5) relative to Q1, even
  after controlling for age, education, sex and sector.
* **Education and place.** Having a course record has an odds ratio of 6.484;
  urban respondents have 1.801 times the odds of rural ones.
* **Does the gap narrow with income?** The Q2-Q4 interactions are not significant
  (p = 0.666, 0.381, 0.155). The Q5 interaction is 1.065 (p = 0.001), so the gap
  is slightly smaller in the richest quintile. Even there the combined female
  effect is about 0.461 x 1.065 = 0.491, so **women's odds remain roughly half
  of men's**. Higher income is associated with a narrower gap, not a closed one.

R-squared is not reported because the outcome is binary; we compare models with
deviance and AIC instead (lower is better).

```{r fit-stats}
models_internet |>
  map(glance) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "model") |>
  select(model, null.deviance, deviance, AIC) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Model fit comparison")
```

**Model fit.** Adding income cuts deviance substantially, and adding age,
education and sector cuts it much further (from 1,262,368 in the sex-only model
to 840,870 in Model 3). The interaction in Model 4 improves fit only slightly
(deviance 840,856), so most of the explanatory power comes from the main
controls.

### Multicollinearity check

Income, sector and education are all related to socio-economic status, so we
check variance inflation factors for Model 3 (VIF is not meaningful in the usual
way once an interaction is included).

```{r vif}
vif(models_internet$model_3_full_controls)
```

All adjusted GVIF values are between about 1.01 and 1.06, far below the usual
concern thresholds (5-10), so the coefficients are not being distorted by
overlap among the predictors.

## Regression 2: economic participation (logistic)

Does the link between digital capability and work depend on income? We add a
capability-by-income interaction.

```{r logit-econ}
model_econ <- glm(
  economically_active == "Yes" ~ capability_tier * mpce_quintile + sex + sector,
  data = reg_data, family = binomial
)

tidy(model_econ, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  mutate(conf.low  = exp(log(estimate) - 1.96 * std.error),
         conf.high = exp(log(estimate) + 1.96 * std.error),
         term = str_replace_all(term, "\n", " ")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Odds ratios: economic participation (age 15+)")

glance(model_econ) |>
  select(null.deviance, deviance, AIC) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Fit statistics")
```

**Reading the model.**

* In the poorest group (Q1) the odds ratios for Medium (0.909) and High (0.936)
  capability are *below 1*: no positive link between digital skill and work.
* The interactions grow with income: for High capability, 1.065 in Q3, 1.228 in
  Q4 and 2.064 in Q5 (all significant). In the richest quintile the combined
  effect is about 0.936 x 2.064 = 1.93, so **highly capable people have roughly
  1.9 times the odds of being economically active** as low-capability people.
* Women have far lower odds of economic participation (odds ratio 0.152,
  p < 0.001) after controlling for capability, income and sector.

This supports the descriptive finding: digital capability is associated with
work mostly where household resources and the local job market let it count.

## Discussion

**Does the gender gap in internet use survive the controls?** Yes. After
controlling for income, age, education and sector, the female odds ratio in
Model 4 is 0.461. The richest-quintile interaction points to some narrowing at
the top, but not closure.

**Does digital capability help work, and only at the top?** The relationship
depends on income. The strongest positive association is for high-capability
people in the richest quintile (interaction odds ratio 2.064). The evidence
points to a conditional relationship, not a uniform effect.

**Policy reading.** Cheaper phones have largely solved *access to a handset*.
What remains is (i) devices that support skilled work, (ii) women's and older
adults' *use* of connectivity inside the household, and (iii) a labour market
that turns digital skill into jobs. These are different problems and need
different tools.

## Limitations

* **Association, not causation.** There is no experimental variation in sex or
  income, and we omit occupation, local labour markets, caste, disability and
  other factors that may affect both digital use and work.
* **Weights and clustering.** The regressions ignore survey weights and the
  clustered design, so standard errors are likely too small and results describe
  the sample. A natural extension is to refit the models with `survey::svyglm()`.
* **Education measure.** `has_course` only records whether a person appears in
  the course file, not years or level of schooling.
* **Capability score.** The four-item score weights each item equally and the
  banking item should be checked against the official questionnaire wording
  before being quoted as "digital banking".
* **Quintiles** are household-level, so everyone in a household shares the same
  income group.

## Key takeaways

1. **Access is bought, and the price differs by device.** Phones are near
   universal; computers are 30 times more common in the richest fifth.
2. **The sex-of-household-head gap is mostly an income gap.**
3. **Income lifts women a long way but never all the way**, and the regression
   confirms the gender gap survives controls (odds ratio 0.46).
4. **The divide is generational as well as economic**: it has closed for rich
   young adults and is widest for middle-aged adults in poor households.
5. **Money buys women connectivity, not work.** Digital inclusion and economic
   inclusion are not the same project.
6. **The digital dividend appears at the top**, where there are jobs that reward
   digital skill.

script are in the project repository. Prepared as coursework for B.A.
